methodological_rigor.justification: The design is a prospective observational cohort analysis nested in the case-control CCGA study with a large sample (n=2,513 stageable invasive cancers) and 5-year follow-up (median 53.8 months), appropriate for the prognostic question. Analysts used an external SEER-matched reference population (age, sex, cancer type, stage) and a one-sample proportional hazards framework (Finkelstein method) with MCMC-based variance estimation for between-group HR comparisons, which is a defensible approach to isolate the signal-detection effect. Weaknesses explicitly acknowledged in the Discussion include lack of control for histology/grade subtypes, treatment, and smoking; use of OS rather than cancer-specific mortality; and probable healthy-volunteer bias that may not be identical between CSD/NCSD groups. No a priori power calculation is reported, and no sensitivity analyses (e.g., removing dominant tumor types like prostate/breast from stage I NCSD) are presented beyond the single prostate reference citation; multiplicity across the 8 stage-specific HR tests is not formally addressed.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The analysis is an individual prospective cohort follow-up of participants enrolled in a case-control validation substudy (CCGA3), with cancer status known at baseline and OS as the endpoint — this maps to Oxford 2b. Clinical relevance is high because MCED tests are an active and controversial screening modality, and the central question — whether ctDNA-detected early-stage cancers are predominantly lethal/micrometastatic (supporting overdiagnosis concerns) or clinically meaningful — directly informs current debates about MCED implementation and FDA/USPSTF deliberations. The patient-relevant endpoint (OS to 5 years) and stage-stratified HRs against a population reference provide actionable prognostic context, though it does not itself change screening guidelines without interventional outcome data.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the appropriate checklist for this observational cohort analysis. Reporting is thorough on most key items: trial registration (NCT02889978), eligibility and recruitment windows, participant flow with exclusions (plasma cell neoplasms, nonstaged, multiple primaries → 310 excluded), outcome definition, follow-up censoring rules, statistical model specification (K-M, one-sample Cox, RStan MCMC, SEER*Stat 8.4.1), and a candid limitations paragraph covering healthy-volunteer bias, lack of subtype matching, missing treatment/smoking data, and OS versus cancer-specific mortality. Gaps include no explicit pre-registration of this specific survival secondary analysis plan versus the parent trial, and no stated data or code availability — in the blinded text there is no repository DOI, GitHub link, or statement about participant-level data access, and SEER inputs are described by version only.

novelty_literature.justification: This is a meaningful extension of a prior analysis (reference 21, CCGA2 with 3-year follow-up and an earlier MCED test version) to the independent validation substudy CCGA3 with a refined assay, longer 5-year follow-up, and an updated one-sample proportional hazards framework matched to SEER. The empirical finding that early-stage CSD cancers have HRs ≈1 relative to SEER-matched references (not worse than conventionally detected cancers) is the main substantive advance and speaks to the active overdiagnosis/micrometastasis debate. It is incremental rather than paradigm-shifting: the conceptual framework, matching approach, and direction of findings replicate the prior CCGA2 report, and no new methodology is introduced beyond the Finkelstein-style one-sample model.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with a self-contained, quantitatively grounded abstract that accurately reflects the headline results (CSD rates 85% vs 34% in dead vs alive; 43% vs 40% and 88% vs 81% observed vs expected OS). Descriptive results subheadings guide the reader through the stage-stratified comparisons, and the Discussion carefully distinguishes the two competing explanations (indolent biology in NCSD vs aggressive biology in CSD) and ties them to prostate-cancer subgroup evidence. Figure captions are standalone-interpretable with group color coding and risk tables noted. Minor issues: some repetition between Abstract/Results on CSD-NCSD proportions, and one typo-like awkwardness ("lived an average age" in Results), but overall clarity is strong.

key_strengths: Large independent validation cohort (n=2,513 stageable invasive cancers) with 5-year follow-up (median 53.8 months) and low loss-to-follow-up (1.5%)
Appropriate one-sample proportional hazards framework matched to SEER on age, sex, cancer type, and stage, with MCMC-based HR comparisons avoiding collinearity among correlated predictors
Clinically important finding that stage I–II CSD cancers have HRs ≈1 versus SEER-matched references, directly addressing the overdiagnosis/micrometastasis debate in MCED screening
Candid limitations section covering healthy-volunteer bias, lack of subtype/treatment/smoking adjustment, and OS versus cancer-specific mortality
Trial registered (NCT02889978); methods well specified with software versions
key_concerns: No pre-specified power calculation or multiplicity correction for the eight stage-stratified HR comparisons
No sensitivity analysis removing dominant indolent tumor types (prostate, breast) from the stage I NCSD group, where the authors concede subtype confounding likely drives the HR 0.51 result
OS rather than cancer-specific mortality limits causal interpretation of the signal-detection effect
No data/code availability statement in the blinded text; participant-level data access and analysis scripts not referenced
Incremental relative to the prior CCGA2 3-year analysis (ref 21) — same conceptual framework, replicated in a different substudy with longer follow-up and a refined classifier
Healthy-volunteer bias acknowledged but not quantified or probed via sensitivity analysis, and may differ between CSD and NCSD groups
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically solid, clinically important validation of MCED prognostic value with a well-matched external reference and transparent limitations, but incremental over the prior CCGA2 report and lacking subtype sensitivity analyses or data/code sharing. Fits Tier 2 (e.g., mid-tier translational oncology journals) with minor revisions to address multiplicity, subtype sensitivity, and reproducibility.
